transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. [Name]. To start, can you tell me what's been bothering you or what brings you in today?

Yeah, um… what’s been bothering me is I feel like I’m constantly moving from one thing to the next. Like I don’t really have an “idle” setting, if that makes sense. Even when nothing urgent is happening, I’m sort of looking for the next thing to do or shifting around, and it’s been harder lately because the new setup at work makes it more obvious.

I work in customer service, and with the way things are arranged now, I can’t really hide it as well. Before, I guess I could sort of blend it in with being busy, but now it feels like I’m always having to manage myself, like trying not to seem like I’m bouncing from task to task or just unable to sit still mentally. It’s not like some huge dramatic crisis, but it’s wearing on me, and I figured maybe I should finally talk to someone about it.
Thinking back, do you remember feeling this same restlessness or difficulty settling into one task when you were a child, say before age 12?

Yeah, I do, actually. I mean, looking back now, it feels like this was around way before this job change. At the time I don’t think anyone called it anything, it was just sort of “that’s how I was.”

In grade school, I remember teachers would say I was bright, like I understood things, but then on report cards or in conferences it would be that I was careless, or I’d rush and miss things, or I needed reminders to stay with my work. And I definitely remember getting told not to talk out of turn. Not in a mean way always, but enough that it was kind of a theme.

So yeah, before 12, for sure. It wasn’t like it suddenly started as an adult. It’s more like I learned little ways to cover it or work around it, and now it’s just harder to do that.
Aside from the restlessness, do you also find it hard to stay focused on a task, follow through on details, or that you often lose track of what you were doing?

Yeah, I do. It’s not like I can’t focus at all, because at the beginning I usually feel like I’m paying attention. Like in the longer coaching meetings at work, or if they give us a new procedure to read, I’ll start off fine and think, okay, I’m following this.

But then a few minutes go by and I realize my eyes have still been moving across the page, or I’ve been nodding along like I’m listening, but I didn’t actually take in what was said. Then I have to kind of back up mentally and think, wait, what did I just miss? It’s frustrating because I’m not trying to ignore it. I know it matters, especially with procedures, but my attention sort of slips without me noticing right away.
Do you often find yourself interrupting others, blurting out answers, or acting before thinking things through, even when you try not to?

Yeah… I do, and I don’t like admitting that because I really don’t mean it in a rude way. It’s more like, if I hear a coworker working through a customer problem — like they’re explaining the issue out loud or trying to figure out what to do next — my brain jumps ahead and I’ll just sort of pop in with the answer before they’ve finished.

Sometimes nobody has even asked me. I’ll hear enough of the situation and think, oh, I know what that is, or oh, we handle that this way, and before I’ve really thought about whether I should speak, I’m already saying it. Then afterward I’ll realize, okay, they weren’t talking to me, or they were still in the middle of getting there themselves.

I try to hold back, especially because I don’t want people to feel like I’m correcting them or taking over, but in the moment it comes out faster than I mean for it to. It’s like the answer is right there and I feel this push to say it before the opening is really there.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports a longstanding pattern (since before age 12) of both inattentive symptoms (losing focus during meetings/reading, missing details despite intending to attend, needing to 're-track' conversations) and hyperactive-impulsive symptoms (constant internal restlessness, inability to be 'idle,' blurting out answers, interrupting coworkers before they finish).
